query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (approximately 1–2 at.%) of aluminum to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enable the in situ formation of a continuous, slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) surface layer during high-temperature exposure, thereby significantly improving oxygen resistance while preserving the alloy’s useful mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, cast HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy by incorporating ~1–2 at.% Al into the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours under low strain rate loading conditions (10−4–10−2 s−1), consistent with prior oxidation-protection studies.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, adherent, continuous Al2O3 (alumina) surface scale induced by the aluminum addition.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, aluminum preferentially segregates to the surface and oxidizes to form an alumina scale. This scale serves as a barrier that slows oxygen ingress into the underlying alloy, preventing rapid oxidation and pesting without significantly altering the bulk microstructure that governs mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-modified HfNbTaTiZr alloy is expected to exhibit markedly improved oxygen resistance—with reduced oxidation kinetics and prevention of pesting—while retaining similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The unmodified equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which experiences detrimental oxidation (pesting) under high-temperature air exposure despite having acceptable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions of air exposure at around 800 °C for a duration of 5 hours and at strain rates on the order of 10−4–10−2 s−1. It assumes that minor compositional adjustment does not compromise the baseline mechanical performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact impact of a 1–2 at.% Al addition on the alloy’s microstructure and mechanical properties is uncertain; there is a risk that even small amounts of Al might subtly alter the bulk properties or the oxidation behavior if the scale formation is incomplete or non-uniform.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of unmodified equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one with an additional 1–2 at.% Al. Subject both sets to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, characterize the surface oxide scales using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess the formation, continuity, and composition of the protective layer. Additionally, perform tensile tests at room temperature and high temperature to compare mechanical properties before and after oxidation exposure.
measurements: Surface oxide scale thickness and phase identification (via XRD, SEM/EDS)
Mass gain measurements as an indicator of oxidation kinetics
Tensile ductility and yield strength at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (around 1000 °C)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-added alloy does not form a continuous and effective alumina scale—indicated by similar or greater oxidation (mass gain) and the presence of non-protective oxide phases—or if there is significant degradation in the mechanical properties compared with the baseline unmodified alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.
